chapter.title: The Object Orientated Interface to SQLite
chapter.para: The object-orientated interface to SQLite provides a number of classes whose methods are used to work with SQLite databases.

The intent is for the object-orientated interface to allow access to the complete functionality and feature set of SQLite. The first release of ooSQLite will not meet, and is not intended to meet, that goal. Lesser used functionality will be added over time.

The object-orientated and classic Rexx interfaces are developed in tandem. As each new feature or functionality of SQLite is added to ooSQLite, access to the feature is added to both interfaces at the same time. There is no SQLite functionality in the object-orientated interface that can not be accessed through the classic Rexx interface. And, vice versa.
The following table lists the classes used in the object orientated interface of the ooSQLite package:

row.entry: The ooSQLite class provieds a number of class methods that are generally useful in working with SQLite databases. Many of the methods are used to query or set values in the database engine rather than an individual database.

An ooSQLiteBackup object provides methods for copying the content of one database into another. It is useful either for creating backups of databases or for copying in-memory databases to or from persistent files.
Each ooSQLiteConnection object represents an open connection to a SQLite database. Mulitple connections to the same database are allowed by instantiating multiple ooSQLiteConnection objects.
The ooSQLiteConstants class provides a CONSTANT value for each SQLite defined constant, and a small number of ooSQLite specific constants.

An ooSQLiteMutex object provides methods for allocating and using a mutex. In general a mutex is a synchronization object used in multi-threading programs to prevent different threads from acessing a shared resource at the same time.
Each ooSQLiteStmt object represents a single SQL statement, which is often referred to as a prepared statment.

section.title: &added11;Callback Methods
section.para: Several methods of the ooSQLiteConnection class register a method of a Rexx object that SQLite invokes later, while it executes SQL: a callback method. They are busyHandler, collationNeeded, commitHook, createCollation, createFunction, profile, progressHandler, rollbackHook, setAuthorizer, trace, and updateHook; exec can also invoke a method for each result row. The arguments of each callback method, and what it must return, are described in the section of each registering method. A callback method must return a whole number, even when its value is ignored, except the step method of an aggregate function; if it returns nothing, a syntax error, 91.999, is raised when the method that executes the SQL returns, and if it returns something else, a syntax error, 98.900.

A condition raised in a callback, and not trapped there, ends the callback, but the program does not get it at once. SQLite is first told to stop where it can: a user defined function sets an error result, so its statement fails; exec stops at that row; the authorizer denies the action; the busy handler gives up; the commit hook turns the commit into a rollback; the progress handler interrupts the operation. The callbacks whose value SQLite ignores can not stop it. The condition is then raised when the method or routine that executes the SQL returns. A SYNTAX condition is raised as itself. Any other condition is raised as a SYNTAX error that keeps the original condition object, as Condition("O") returns it, as the second item of its additional array: HALT as error 4.1, "Program interrupted with HALT condition", as an untrapped HALT is, and any other condition, such as USER or ERROR, as error 98.900, for example The USER BOOM condition was raised in the callback "cb": description. A program traps them with SIGNAL ON SYNTAX around the method or routine that executes the SQL, not with SIGNAL ON USER.

A callback runs on the thread that executes the SQL, which need not be the thread that registered it, and the condition reaches that thread. Before ooSQLite 1.1, a condition raised in a callback that ran on a thread other than the one that registered it, SYNTAX included, was lost: that thread only got the result code of SQLite.

The reason is that a SIGNAL to a trap in the caller would have to leave SQLite in the middle of its work. Before ooSQLite 1.1, a condition other than SYNTAX raised in a callback method did reach a SIGNAL ON trap in the caller as itself, but it left the statement SQLite was running unfinalized, so that the connection could not be closed, and the mutex of the connection held, so that another thread that used the connection hung the process; in a callback routine it was lost. The condition of a callback was also printed to the standard output, even when the program trapped it; it is not printed any more.
